title: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) in a patient with post streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN): A case report
case_prompt:
An 8-year-old boy with known β-thalassemia intermedia presented with 6 days of generalized body swelling, 3 days of fever, and 1 day of seizures.  
- Vital signs: temperature 39.0°C, blood pressure 145/76 mmHg, heart rate 115 beats/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.  
- General: pale child with “chipmunk” facies, periorbital and generalized edema.  
- Chest and cardiovascular exams were unremarkable.  
- Neurologic: Glasgow Coma Scale 12 (E4V3M5), no neck stiffness; motor tone normal, strength 4/5 in all limbs, reflexes 2+.  
- Growth parameters: weight −3 SD, height −2 SD for age.  
- History: untreated sore throat in the preceding week; up-to-date vaccinations except no COVID-19 vaccine.  
In the emergency department, he experienced a brief tonic–clonic seizure with urinary incontinence and postictal drowsiness, treated with IV diazepam and levetiracetam.  
A working differential diagnosis included hypertensive encephalopathy in the setting of thalassemia, renal artery stenosis, meningoencephalitis, and acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Hypertensive encephalopathy was considered because of acute hypertension and seizure — “a differential diagnosis of thalassemia with hypertensive encephalopathy…was established.”  
2. Renal artery stenosis was included for new-onset hypertension and edema — “a differential diagnosis of…renal artery stenosis…was established.”  
3. Meningoencephalitis was considered in light of fever and seizure activity — “a differential diagnosis of…meningoencephalitis…was established.”  
4. Acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis was confirmed by serologic and urinary findings — “Urine and blood analysis…revealed…elevated antistreptococcal titer in blood, low complement levels in serum, and a significant presence of RBCs in urine, ultimately confirming the diagnosis of APSGN.”  
5. Acute disseminated demyelinating encephalomyelitis was supported by neuroimaging — “These findings supported the diagnosis of acute disseminated demyelinated encephalomyelitis (ADEM).”
